title: APPLE: General Active Perception via RL
one_liner: Train a robot to decide what to sense next by jointly learning where to look and what it sees, using rewards instead of hand-written rules.
lead: A robot touching an object only feels one small patch at a time, so it must choose where to explore next. Most methods tell the robot exactly how to explore (look for the shape, maximize information gain), but this locks them to one task. APPLE learns a decision policy and a perception module together from reward signals, letting the same robot solve grasping, pose estimation, classification, or anything else.

problem.h2: Robots see one tiny piece at a time
paras: A robot's gripper has a touch sensor smaller than your fingertip. When it explores an object, each contact reads only that one spot, not the whole shape. The robot must decide: move left? right? press harder? Current methods solve this by hand-coding the goal (find the shape, maximize information gain for grasping), so each robot program is built for one job.

A beginner would try: let the robot randomly poke until it learns. This fails because random poking takes thousands of touches and never finds a strategy—the robot wastes time on useless spots. The real gap is that no method lets one robot solve multiple tasks by learning what to sense from rewards alone.

callout.html: Current active perception methods are locked to one task with hand-coded objectives; they do not learn a general policy for deciding where to sense next.

steps.text: The perception module reads all touches collected so far and predicts the object's properties (shape, pose, class).
The decision policy looks at the current prediction and outputs the best sensor move (direction, force, contact point) using reinforcement learning.
The robot makes that move, the sensor reads a new patch, and the environment gives a reward (progress toward the goal).
Both the perception module and policy learn from the new observation and reward via a shared neural network backbone, using one loss function.
Repeat steps 1-4 until the robot's prediction is accurate enough to grasp, estimate pose, or classify correctly.

object.h2: What changes: the joint training objective
paras: APPLE does not hand-code a task-specific objective like maximize information gain. Instead, it treats active perception as a reinforcement learning problem: the policy learns to move the sensor by maximizing a reward signal, and the perception module learns to predict from the sensor history. Both modules share a deep neural network backbone (which reads sequences of sensor touches) and train together on the same reward.

hidden.h2: The hidden quantity: expected future reward
hidden.name: expected future reward per move
paras: As the robot explores, each sensor move opens different futures. Some moves lead to fast, accurate predictions; others waste time. The policy must learn which move is most valuable right now—that is, which move will bring the highest total reward across all remaining steps. This is the expected future reward, and the paper estimates it by running episodes and measuring how quickly each move sequence reaches the goal.

The policy learns to rank moves by their expected future value using a model based on a transformer architecture (which reads a sequence of sensor touches and outputs predictions). High-value moves (those that narrow down the object's properties fastest) get chosen first. The perception module feeds into this ranking by outputting the current best guess, which helps the policy decide what to sense next.

heat.caption: Darker moves bring faster, more accurate predictions. Policy learns to prefer them.

reads.html: Every move choice is a bet: some bets pay off quickly (learn the object fast), others waste time. The policy learns which bets are good for each stage of exploration.

The paper estimates expected future reward via policy gradient: the gradient of the policy's log-likelihood weighted by the cumulative discounted reward, capturing how each move contributes to task success.

mechanism.h2: Why it works: shared learning breaks the task lock
paras: Old methods tie the robot to one task by hand-coding the objective (find shape, maximize information gain). APPLE breaks this lock by learning from reward signals instead. Because both the perception module and policy train on the same transformer backbone and use the same reward, they learn to cooperate: the perception module gets better at reading the sensor data, and the policy gets better at choosing moves that maximize the shared reward.

This generality comes from abstraction. The neural network backbone learns to represent sensor history in a flexible way—not optimized for shape or pose or class, but for whatever the reward signals (the task goal) demands. The policy then learns to steer exploration by this flexible representation. Change the reward from grasping to pose estimation to classification, and the same trained modules adapt because they learned a general strategy: gather high-value information.

stages.s: Policy ranks next moves by expected reward

math.words: change to policy weights equals expected value of (log likelihood of chosen move times cumulative discounted future reward)
math.equation: dtheta_policy = E[(dtheta log pi(a|o)) * sum_t gamma^t reward_t]
symbols: which direction to nudge the policy weights to increase total reward
probability the policy chooses move a given current observation o
which way to nudge weights so this move becomes more likely
discount factor (typically 0.99), weights immediate rewards more than far-future ones
the signal at step t (how close we are to solving the task)
total future reward from now on, with older rewards weighted less

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose the policy chooses move Right at step 0, and the robot then gets rewards: step 0 = +1.0 (small progress), step 1 = +2.0 (bigger progress), step 2 = +1.5 (slight progress). Cumulative (gamma=0.99): 1.0 + 0.99*2.0 + 0.99^2*1.5 = 1.0 + 1.98 + 1.48 = 4.46.
If log probability of Right is +0.5 (the policy was confident), the gradient is 0.5 * 4.46 = 2.23. This nudges the weights to make Right even more likely in similar future situations.

If a different move Up had been tried with the same observation and gotten total reward 2.0, then gradient for Up is 0.5 * 2.0 = 1.0—the weights pull less strongly toward Up, because it yielded lower total reward.

math.note: The policy learns to increase the probability of high-reward moves and decrease the probability of low-reward moves, automatically trading off exploration and exploitation without hand-coded heuristics.

items.b: Sensor gets stuck in local optima.
items.html: If the robot learns a lazy exploration strategy early (poke only in one spot), the policy may not explore enough to solve harder tasks. Early random exploration or a curriculum (start with simple tasks) helps because random moves keep the policy from settling into a dead-end strategy, and easy tasks let the policy find a good foundation before facing complexity.

items.b: Reward signal too sparse or unclear.
items.html: If the reward only fires at the very end (binary: solved or not), the policy takes too long to learn which moves help. Shaping the reward (give small +0.1 for progress) accelerates learning because frequent, small rewards act like stepping stones—the policy can see which moves nudge it closer to the goal right away, instead of waiting hundreds of steps for one big signal.

items.b: Perception module overfits to training objects.
items.html: If the robot trains only on wooden blocks, it may fail on rubber or cloth because the touch signal shifts. Training on diverse materials helps because the perception module must learn which features matter (stiffness, texture, shape) across many surfaces, so it builds a more general predictor that works on unseen materials.
With a well-shaped reward, diverse training data, and enough exploration noise, APPLE learns a policy that works on new tasks and new objects it has not seen before.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Implement APPLE on a simulated tactile robot (or the Tactile MNIST benchmark, a standard test set where the goal is to classify digits 0-9 by touch alone). Train the policy and perception module jointly for 10,000 episodes. Then swap the reward signal from classification (maximize correct digit predictions) to pose estimation (minimize angle error), and fine-tune for 1,000 episodes. The demo should show that the same robot policy solves both tasks, adapting its exploration strategy purely from the new reward, proving that APPLE breaks the task lock.
demo.metric_eq: task_generality = (accuracy_task_A after training on task_A + accuracy_task_B after fine_tuning on task_B) / 2, compared to task-specific baselines on each task separately
demo.closing: The core proof: one robot, one learned policy, two different tasks—achieved by removing hand-coded objectives and letting reward signals teach exploration strategy.
